questions.stem: What is a democracy?
options: A system where an unelected council governs on citizens' behalf
A system where citizens choose their government through free elections
A system where only property owners are entitled to vote
A system where elections are held but only one party may stand
questions.explanation: The defining feature is that political power derives from the people through elections.

questions.stem: What is the Australian Constitution?
options: A treaty with another country
The founding legal document setting out how Australia is governed
A list of all Australian laws
A statement of Australian values with no legal force
questions.explanation: It establishes the Commonwealth and divides power between federal and state governments.

questions.stem: How many houses does the Australian federal Parliament have?
options: One
Three
Four
Two
questions.explanation: The House of Representatives and the Senate. This is called a bicameral parliament.
questions.teaching:
The Commonwealth Parliament is bicameral, meaning it has two chambers, and a bill must pass both to become law.

The lower chamber is where government is formed, by whichever party holds a majority of its seats. The upper chamber represents the states equally, with the same number of senators from each regardless of population — a condition the smaller colonies insisted on before agreeing to federate. Not every Australian parliament works this way: Queensland abolished its second chamber in 1922.

questions.stem: What is the House of Representatives sometimes called?
options: The cabinet
The lower house
The upper house
The high court
questions.explanation: The Senate is the upper house.
questions.teaching:
Each chamber of Parliament has a formal name and an informal one, and both get used.

The chamber where government is formed is the larger of the two, elected from single-member electorates of roughly equal population, and it is where most legislation begins. It is informally called by a term describing its position in the traditional arrangement of a parliament. The other chamber gets the opposite label. State parliaments use different formal names for the same two roles.

questions.stem: Who becomes Prime Minister of Australia?
options: The longest-serving member of parliament
The leader of the party or coalition with majority support in the House of Representatives
The person who receives the most individual votes nationwide
The person appointed by the High Court
questions.explanation: Australians vote for local members, not directly for a Prime Minister.

questions.stem: What is the role of the Governor-General?
options: To lead the government day to day
To decide court cases
To lead the opposition
To represent the monarch and perform formal constitutional duties
questions.explanation: The role is largely ceremonial, with reserve powers exercised only in exceptional circumstances.

questions.stem: What is a bill in parliament?
options: A court decision
A government budget only
A proposed law being considered by parliament
A law that has already passed
questions.explanation: A bill becomes an Act once passed by both houses and given royal assent.

questions.stem: What is statutory law?
options: Law from another country
Unwritten custom
Law made by parliament
Law made by judges through court decisions
questions.explanation: Parliament makes statute law; courts develop common law.
questions.teaching:
Australian law comes from two main sources, and they work differently.

One is made by elected parliaments, written down in Acts, and can be changed by passing another Act. The other is built up by judges deciding cases, where each decision binds lower courts in similar future cases — this is common law or case law. Where the two conflict, the parliamentary source prevails, because parliament can legislate to override a court's interpretation. Knowing which source a rule came from tells you how it can be changed.

questions.stem: What is common law?
options: Law developed through decisions made by judges in courts
Law passed by parliament
Law that applies only to common people
International law
questions.explanation: Common law builds through precedent — earlier decisions guiding later ones.

questions.stem: What is the rule of law?
options: The principle that the government can change any law instantly
The rule that judges make all laws
The idea that laws apply only to citizens
The principle that everyone, including governments, is subject to the law
questions.explanation: No one is above the law — the core of the principle.
questions.teaching:
The idea is old and blunt: the law applies to the powerful in exactly the way it applies to everyone else. A prime minister who steals is a thief. A police officer who assaults somebody has committed assault.

Several practical requirements follow. Laws must be published, so people can know what they are. They generally cannot be applied backwards in time, since nobody can obey a rule that did not yet exist. Disputes must be settled by independent courts rather than by the body being complained about. The contrast is rule *by* law, where those in charge use legislation as a tool against others while standing outside it themselves. The two phrases are nearly identical and the difference between them is the whole point.

questions.stem: What is voting like in Australian federal elections?
options: Compulsory only for those over 25
Compulsory for enrolled citizens aged 18 and over
Optional for all citizens
Restricted to property owners
questions.explanation: Australia is one of relatively few democracies with compulsory voting.

questions.stem: What is criminal law concerned with?
options: Offences against society that the state prosecutes
Disputes between individuals over contracts
The division of powers between governments
Elections and voting
questions.explanation: Civil law handles disputes between parties; criminal law handles offences prosecuted by the state.

questions.stem: What is civil law concerned with?
options: The Constitution only
International treaties only
Disputes between individuals or organisations
Crimes prosecuted by the state
questions.explanation: Civil matters include contracts, negligence and property disputes.

questions.stem: What is a political party?
options: A court
A group of public servants
An organised group with shared views that seeks to win government
A government department
questions.explanation: Parties select candidates and contest elections on a shared platform.

questions.stem: What is an independent representative?
options: An elected member who does not belong to a political party
A public servant
A judge
A member of the Senate only
questions.explanation: Independents can hold significant influence when no party has a majority.

questions.stem: What does 'secular' mean when describing Australian democracy?
options: Government is separate from religious institutions
Religion is banned
Only one religion is permitted
Government is run by religious leaders
questions.explanation: Secular means separation, not hostility to religion. Australians remain free to practise any faith.

questions.stem: What is a referendum in Australia?
options: A national vote to change the Constitution
An ordinary federal election
A vote in parliament
A court decision
questions.explanation: Changing the Constitution requires a referendum, which must achieve a double majority.
questions.teaching:
The Constitution is deliberately difficult to alter. Parliament can pass an ordinary law with a simple majority, but it cannot rewrite the founding document that way — the people themselves have to agree.

The bar is set high. A proposal must pass both houses, then go to every voter, and then clear a double majority: more than half of all voters nationally, and a majority in at least four of the six states. That second requirement stops the smaller states being overruled by New South Wales and Victoria between them. It also explains the record — of 45 proposals put since 1901, only eight have got through. Do not confuse it with a plebiscite, which asks the public a question without altering the founding document at all.

questions.stem: What does 'multi-faith society' mean?
options: A society with no religion
A society where religion determines the law
A society in which people of many different religions live together
A society with one official religion
questions.explanation: Australia's population includes many faiths and people of no faith.

questions.stem: What is one way a citizen can influence lawmaking?
options: Contacting their elected representative
Ignoring elections
Refusing to pay taxes
Only by becoming a judge
questions.explanation: Contacting representatives, petitions, lobby groups and public campaigns are all legitimate avenues.

questions.stem: What is the role of the courts?
options: To run elections
To lead the government
To interpret and apply the law, and resolve disputes
To make all new laws
questions.explanation: Courts interpret; parliament legislates. This separation is a feature of the system.

questions.stem: Why does Australia have two houses of parliament?
options: To double the number of politicians
Because the Constitution could not decide
To separate state and federal law
The Senate reviews legislation and represents the states, providing a check on the lower house
questions.explanation: The Senate acts as a house of review and gives each state equal representation regardless of population.

questions.stem: What does the separation of powers refer to?
options: Dividing power between the parliament, the executive and the judiciary
Dividing power between states
Dividing votes between parties
Separating criminal and civil law
questions.explanation: Each branch checks the others, which limits the concentration of power.

questions.stem: Why is an independent judiciary important?
options: Judges can apply the law without political pressure, including against the government
It allows judges to make any law they wish
It removes the need for parliament
It speeds up elections
questions.explanation: Independence is what allows courts to rule against the government of the day.

questions.stem: What is a double majority in a referendum?
options: A majority in every single state
A majority of voters nationally and a majority in a majority of states
Twice as many yes votes as no votes
A majority in both houses of parliament
questions.explanation: The requirement is deliberately demanding, which is why most referendums fail.

questions.stem: How does compulsory voting affect Australian democracy?
options: It makes preference flows predictable, which is what allows results to be called on election night
It produces high turnout, so results reflect the whole electorate rather than the most motivated
It requires every voter to be enrolled, which keeps the electoral roll more accurate than elsewhere
It prevents parties from campaigning on turnout, so they compete on policy detail instead
questions.explanation: Turnout above 90% is typical, compared with much lower figures in voluntary systems.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a lobby group?
options: To advocate for a particular interest and influence government decisions
To run elections
To interpret the law
To collect taxes
questions.explanation: Lobby groups are a legitimate form of participation, though their influence is debated.

questions.stem: Why is freedom of speech considered important in a democracy?
options: It allows any statement to be made provided it is sincerely held
It applies during election campaigns in particular
It ensures the media reports all sides equally
Citizens need to be able to criticise government and debate ideas openly
questions.explanation: The freedom is not unlimited — defamation and incitement laws apply — but open criticism is essential to accountability.

questions.stem: How can a court decision effectively change the law?
options: Courts can repeal Acts of Parliament at will
Court decisions never affect law
A higher court's interpretation sets a precedent that lower courts must follow
Judges vote on new statutes
questions.explanation: Precedent is how common law develops. Parliament can override it with new legislation.

questions.stem: What is the place of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander customary law in Australia?
options: It continues to have cultural authority within communities and is recognised in limited legal contexts
It was formally incorporated into Australian law at Federation and operates alongside the common law
It applies only in the Northern Territory, where it was given statutory force in the 1970s
It was replaced entirely by the common law, though it retains standing in ceremonial matters
questions.explanation: The curriculum names customary law alongside criminal and civil law. Its recognition in the Australian legal system is partial and varies by context.

questions.stem: How do democratic values support social cohesion?
options: They apply only during elections
Shared commitments to fairness and respect help diverse groups coexist
They require everyone to hold identical beliefs
They prevent any disagreement
questions.explanation: The curriculum links freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity to a resilient democracy.

questions.stem: Why might a government with a majority in the lower house still fail to pass a bill?
options: Courts vote on bills
It may lack the numbers in the Senate
Bills only need lower house approval
The Governor-General routinely refuses bills
questions.explanation: Both houses must pass a bill, and governments often lack a Senate majority.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the executive and the parliament?
options: The executive is part of the judiciary
Parliament makes laws; the executive government administers and implements them
They are the same body
The executive makes laws and parliament implements them
questions.explanation: In Australia the executive is drawn from parliament, which is why the separation is less strict than in some systems.

questions.stem: Why is the Constitution difficult to change by design?
options: Because no one understands it
To prevent citizens from voting
Because it cannot be amended at all
Fundamental rules should not shift with ordinary political majorities
questions.explanation: Entrenchment provides stability. The trade-off is that even widely supported reforms can fail.

questions.stem: Why does the balance of power in the Senate matter to minor parties and independents?
options: When no party holds a majority, their votes decide whether legislation passes
They control the House of Representatives
They appoint the Prime Minister
They can veto court decisions
questions.explanation: Holding the balance of power gives disproportionate influence relative to seat numbers.

questions.stem: A citizen argues laws should reflect majority opinion without limit. What is the strongest counter?
options: Majority opinion changes too quickly to legislate on, so laws would need rewriting every few months
Most citizens do not follow legislation closely enough for their opinion to be properly informed
Parliament already represents the majority, so testing opinion separately would duplicate its work
Unlimited majority rule can override the rights of minorities, which democratic principles also protect
questions.explanation: Constitutional limits and rights protections exist precisely to constrain what a majority may do — a genuine tension within democratic theory.

questions.stem: How do the principles of the legal system protect a person accused of a crime?
options: The right to refuse to attend court, to decline to answer and to have the charge withdrawn
Presumption of innocence, the right to a fair hearing and the burden of proof on the prosecution
The right to select a judge, to see the evidence in advance and to appeal any verdict at all
A guarantee of legal representation paid by the state in every criminal matter, whatever its size
questions.explanation: These principles protect against wrongful conviction; they do not guarantee any particular outcome.

questions.stem: Why is it argued that a free press strengthens democracy?
options: It guarantees all reporting is accurate
It replaces the need for elections
It controls what parliament may debate
It informs citizens and scrutinises those in power, supporting accountability
questions.explanation: Scrutiny is the mechanism. Accuracy is not guaranteed, which is why media literacy matters alongside press freedom.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence that a country's institutions reflect democratic values?
options: The existence of a written constitution alone
A high number of laws
Frequent changes of leader
Regular free elections, an independent judiciary, and governments that leave office when defeated
questions.explanation: The transfer of power after defeat is the practical test. A constitution on paper is not sufficient on its own.

questions.stem: Why might different citizens hold different views of Australian national identity?
options: Identity is shaped by heritage, experience and connection to place, which vary widely
There is only one correct national identity
National identity is defined in law
Identity does not vary between people
questions.explanation: The curriculum notes diverse experiences and perspectives on citizenship and identity, including the distinct connections of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

questions.stem: A proposed law is popular but may conflict with the Constitution. What can happen?
options: Parliament can pass it and amend the Constitution afterwards
The Governor-General decides its validity
The High Court can rule it invalid if it exceeds constitutional power
A strong majority in both houses overrides constitutional limits
questions.explanation: Constitutional review by the High Court is a key check on legislative power.

questions.stem: What is the opposition in parliament?
options: The upper house
A committee of judges
The largest party or coalition not in government
A group of independents only
questions.explanation: The opposition scrutinises the government and offers an alternative.

questions.stem: What is a ballot?
options: A court hearing
A political party
The paper or process by which a vote is cast
A parliamentary debate
questions.explanation: A secret ballot protects voters from pressure.
questions.teaching:
Voting has its own vocabulary, and the terms describe different parts of the process.

Enrolment is registering to vote. An electorate is the area a member represents. A polling place is where voting happens. And one term covers the means by which a vote is actually cast and recorded — historically a small ball, which is where the word comes from, and now the paper you fill in. The secrecy of it is what protects voters from pressure, and it is why compulsory attendance cannot become compulsory choosing.

questions.stem: What is a cabinet?
options: The senior ministers who make key government decisions
All members of parliament
The judges of the High Court
A parliamentary committee of the opposition
questions.explanation: Cabinet is drawn from the governing party's senior members.

questions.stem: What is the High Court of Australia?
options: A state court
The highest court, which interprets the Constitution
The court that hears all criminal trials first
A parliamentary committee
questions.explanation: It is the final court of appeal and rules on constitutional questions.

questions.stem: What does 'preferential voting' mean?
options: Voting is optional
Voters rank candidates in order of preference
Voters choose only one candidate
Only party leaders vote
questions.explanation: Preferences are distributed until a candidate has a majority.

questions.stem: What is a minister responsible for?
options: Writing the Constitution
A particular area of government, such as health or education
Judging court cases
Running elections
questions.explanation: Ministers head portfolios and are accountable to parliament.

questions.stem: What is federation in the Australian context?
options: The creation of the High Court
The introduction of compulsory voting
The joining of the colonies into one nation in 1901
The separation of church and state
questions.explanation: Federation created the Commonwealth of Australia under the Constitution.

questions.stem: What is a local council responsible for?
options: Local services such as waste, roads and planning
Schools and public hospitals
Criminal law and the police force
State roads and public transport
questions.explanation: Australia has three levels of government, each with different responsibilities.

questions.stem: Why does Australia have three levels of government?
options: Because the colonies could not agree on a single parliament
To give each state an equal share of national power
Different issues are best handled at local, state and national scales
To separate lawmaking from law enforcement
questions.explanation: Responsibilities are divided so decisions are made at an appropriate scale.

questions.stem: What happens if a state law conflicts with a valid federal law?
options: The federal law prevails to the extent of the inconsistency
The state law prevails
Both are cancelled
The courts cannot decide
questions.explanation: This is set out in the Constitution and is a key feature of the federal system.

questions.stem: Why is the secret ballot important?
options: It lets voters see how others have voted
It removes the need to enrol before an election
It allows a vote to be changed after it is cast
Voters can choose freely without fear of intimidation
questions.explanation: The secret ballot is sometimes called the Australian ballot because of its early adoption here.

questions.stem: How does preferential voting differ from first-past-the-post?
options: It is used only in the Senate
The winner must gain a majority after preferences, not just the most first votes
It requires fewer candidates
It means voters cannot rank candidates
questions.explanation: It reduces the chance of a candidate winning with a small minority of support.

questions.stem: Why are courts described as independent of parliament?
options: Judges are elected by parliament
Courts write legislation
Courts report to ministers
Judges decide cases on law and evidence, not on government instruction
questions.explanation: Independence allows courts to rule against the government, which is the point.

questions.stem: What does 'equality before the law' mean?
options: Everyone receives the same sentence
Everyone must know all laws
Laws are decided by public vote
The law applies to everyone in the same way regardless of status
questions.explanation: It concerns equal application, not identical outcomes in every case.

questions.stem: Why is the presumption of innocence important?
options: It places the burden of proof on the prosecution, protecting against wrongful conviction
It means the accused is always innocent
It speeds up trials
It applies only to civil cases
questions.explanation: Requiring the state to prove guilt is a fundamental safeguard.

questions.stem: What is the significance of a government losing a vote of no confidence?
options: It indicates the government has lost the support of the house and may have to resign or call an election
The government must call a referendum on the issue
The courts take over
The Senate becomes the government
questions.explanation: Confidence of the lower house is what sustains a government in this system.

questions.stem: Why are most referendums in Australia unsuccessful?
options: Referendums require unanimous agreement between the states
The wording is always unclear
The double majority is demanding and bipartisan support is often absent
Referendums can only be held alongside a federal election
questions.explanation: Only eight of forty-five proposals have succeeded, and those usually had support across the major parties.

questions.stem: Which argument best supports compulsory voting?
options: It ensures results reflect the whole electorate rather than only the highly motivated
It guarantees better governments
It makes counting easier
It removes the need for campaigns
questions.explanation: The case rests on representativeness. Critics argue it compels uninformed votes, which is a genuine counter-argument.

questions.stem: How do common law and statute law interact?
options: Parliament can pass legislation that overrides or codifies judge-made law
They never interact
Common law overrides statute
Courts write statutes
questions.explanation: Parliament is supreme within its constitutional powers, but courts interpret what statutes mean.

questions.stem: What is a democracy's basic principle regarding power?
options: Political authority comes from the people
Power rests with whoever commands the armed forces
Power is exercised by officials appointed on merit
Power is divided equally between the states
questions.explanation: Elections are the mechanism through which that authority is exercised.

questions.stem: What is a law?
options: A social custom
A political opinion
A government policy proposal
A rule enforced by the state that applies to everyone
questions.explanation: Laws are enforceable; customs and policies are not in the same way.
questions.teaching:
Rules come in several kinds and they differ in who makes them and what happens if you break them.

A school rule applies within a school. A social custom carries no formal penalty. A moral principle is a belief about right conduct. And one kind is made through a recognised process, applies to everyone in the jurisdiction, and is enforced by the state through courts and penalties. That enforcement by the state, applying to all rather than to members of a group, is what marks it out.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a policy and a law?
options: Policy is made by courts
Policy is a plan of action; law is an enforceable rule
They are identical
Policy is enforceable and law is not
questions.explanation: Governments implement policy, which may or may not require legislation.

questions.stem: What is a jury?
options: A panel of judges
A committee of parliament
A group of lawyers
A group of citizens who decide the facts in some trials
questions.explanation: Juries determine guilt in serious criminal trials; judges decide the law and sentence.
questions.teaching:
Court cases divide the work between two roles, and keeping them separate is a principle of the system.

One role decides questions of law: what the rules mean, what evidence is admissible, and what sentence applies. That belongs to the judge. The other decides questions of fact — what actually happened, and whether the case has been proved — and in serious criminal matters that is given to a group of ordinary citizens selected at random. The point of using citizens is that the community, not the state alone, decides guilt.

questions.stem: What does the Australian Electoral Commission do?
options: Chooses candidates
Writes electoral laws
Appoints the Prime Minister
Conducts federal elections independently of government
questions.explanation: Independence of the electoral body is important for trust in results.

questions.stem: What is enrolment to vote?
options: Standing as a candidate
Registering on the electoral roll so you can vote
Voting in an election
Joining a political party
questions.explanation: Enrolment is compulsory for eligible Australians aged 18 and over.

questions.stem: What is a preamble in a constitution?
options: A list of laws
A court judgement
A political party platform
An introductory statement setting out purpose
questions.explanation: Preambles express intent rather than create enforceable rights.
questions.teaching:
Constitutions are structured documents, and the opening section does a particular job.

Before the operative provisions begin, many constitutions open with a statement setting out who is establishing the document and why — its purposes and the values behind it. It is usually not enforceable in itself, but courts may look to it when interpreting the sections that follow. Australia's is short and was drafted in the 1890s; proposals to add recognition of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples to it have been debated for decades.

questions.stem: What is a by-election?
options: A general election
A referendum
A local council vote
An election held to fill a single seat that becomes vacant
questions.explanation: By-elections occur between general elections when a member resigns or dies.
questions.teaching:
Elections happen on a fixed cycle, but seats can fall vacant between them through death, resignation or disqualification.

When that happens the seat is filled by an election in that electorate alone, rather than waiting for the next general election or appointing someone. Only the voters of that one electorate take part. Because these are often treated as a verdict on the government of the day, they attract attention out of proportion to the single seat at stake.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'the Crown' in the Australian system?
options: The monarch as head of state, represented by the Governor-General
The Prime Minister
The High Court
The Senate
questions.explanation: Australia is a constitutional monarchy with the monarch's role largely formal.

questions.stem: What does 'bicameral' mean?
options: Having two houses of parliament
Having two political parties
Having two levels of court
Having two elections a year
questions.explanation: The Australian federal parliament and most states are bicameral.

questions.stem: Why is an independent electoral commission important?
options: It reduces the cost of elections
It prevents the governing party from influencing how elections are run
It selects the winner
It writes the laws
questions.explanation: Independence underpins confidence that results reflect the vote.

questions.stem: Why does the Constitution divide powers between federal and state governments?
options: To let each level raise its own taxes independently
Because the colonies had different legal systems
To ensure federal law always overrides state law
So responsibilities are exercised at an appropriate level and power is not concentrated
questions.explanation: The division was central to the bargain that created the federation.

questions.stem: How can a citizen challenge a law they believe is unconstitutional?
options: Ask parliament to vote again
Refuse to obey it with no consequence
Contact the Governor-General
Bring a case before the courts, ultimately the High Court
questions.explanation: Judicial review is how constitutional limits are enforced.

questions.stem: Why is the right to a fair trial considered fundamental?
options: It guarantees acquittal
It speeds up justice
It applies only to serious crimes
It protects individuals against the state's much greater power
questions.explanation: The imbalance of resources between state and individual is why safeguards exist.

questions.stem: Why might a government hold a plebiscite rather than a referendum?
options: Plebiscites change the Constitution
They are the same thing
Plebiscites are legally binding always
A plebiscite tests opinion without changing the Constitution
questions.explanation: Only a referendum can alter the Constitution; a plebiscite gauges views.

questions.stem: What role does the media play in a democracy?
options: Running elections
Appointing judges
Informing citizens and scrutinising those in power
Making laws
questions.explanation: The scrutiny function is why press freedom is linked to accountability.

questions.stem: Why does Australia have both criminal and civil law?
options: Criminal law is for businesses only
They address different wrongs: offences against society and disputes between parties
One replaced the other
They are identical in practice
questions.explanation: The standard of proof and who brings the case differ between them.

questions.stem: Why is the independence of the Australian Electoral Commission in drawing boundaries significant?
options: It prevents electorates being drawn to favour a party
It reduces the number of voters
It determines who may stand
Boundaries are redrawn by the governing party after each census
questions.explanation: Independent redistribution guards against gerrymandering.

questions.stem: Why can protecting minority rights sometimes conflict with majority rule?
options: Minority rights are protected only by convention
A majority decision is binding on the courts
Minority rights apply only to citizens
A majority may support measures that disadvantage a minority
questions.explanation: Constitutional limits and courts exist partly to manage this tension.

questions.stem: How does the concept of the rule of law constrain a government?
options: The rule of law binds ministers but not departments
It requires every law to be approved by the courts first
Government must act within existing law and can be challenged in court
Government may act first and legislate afterwards
questions.explanation: Legality of executive action is testable in the courts.

questions.stem: Why are constitutional conventions important even though they are unwritten?
options: They are legally enforceable
They are written in the Constitution
They have no role
Much of how the system actually operates depends on them being followed
questions.explanation: The Governor-General acting on ministerial advice is a convention, not a written rule.
